warmup.q: The counting program from the opening now uses its tool's exactly-once setting, for its counts and for the results it writes out. When a card's count reaches 10, it still emails the cardholder. The machine crashes, and the program starts again from its last saved point. How many emails can one card get?
options: Exactly one: the program is set to exactly-once
At most one: the saved point remembers which emails went out
One or more: the payments after the saved point are handled again, email included
None: emails sent since the saved point are taken back with everything else
warmup.why: Exactly-once covers the program's own state, what it remembers between payments, and the results it hands out through one careful exit, called the sink. After a crash, the program goes back to its last saved point and handles the payments since then a second time. If one of them takes a card to 10, the email goes out again, and nothing can take back an email. The fourth section measures it: 135 emails where 90 were due. The fix is to send the email request out through the sink, with a key the mail service checks so that it acts once. The first option is the trap: the setting's name promises more than it covers.

sections.h: Starting again after a crash: easy for a batch job, hard for a stream
sections.html:
Payments arrive all day and never stop. They wait in a log kept by Kafka, a program that stores messages in the order they arrive and lets other programs read them from any position. Each payment is a record in that log, and its position is its offset: 0 for the first, 1 for the next, and so on. A program that reads records as they arrive and works something out from them, here a count per card, is called a stream processor.

Compare it with a batch job, a program that works through a fixed pile of input in one run, such as adding up yesterday's payments at night. A batch job that dies halfway is easy to recover: throw away its half-written output and run it again. The input hasn't changed, each part of the job writes its own file, and the output becomes visible only when the whole job has succeeded. Some records were handled twice, but every record's effect appears once. That's the meaning of "exactly-once" worth keeping: effectively once.

A stream processor can't wait for the end, because there is no end. After a crash, three things must come back in agreement. One is the input position, the offset it had reached. One is its state, what it remembers between records, such as the count for each card. And one is the output the world has already seen. To commit something is to write it down for good, so a crash can't undo it.

The Messaging track's lesson Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees showed what happens when only two agree. Commit the offset before handling the records, and a crash loses the ones in between (at-most-once). Commit after, and a crash handles every record since the last commit again (at-least-once).

Let's watch at-least-once go wrong. Our first version writes one row per payment into a results table the moment it handles it, and commits its offset after every 100 payments. In the Try it, it handles 1,000 payments and crashes right after writing the row for payment 950. Its last committed offset was 900, so it starts again there and writes rows 900 to 950 a second time: 1,051 rows for 1,000 payments, 51 of them twice.

The first fix turns the stream into small batch jobs. Micro-batching cuts the input into batches by offset range, such as payments 900 to 999, and keeps each batch's rows in memory. When the batch ends, it makes the rows and the end offset durable together, in one step. Durable means saved on disk, where a crash can't wipe it. A crash mid-batch leaves nothing of that batch visible, and the rerun reads the same offsets again. In the Try it, this version ends with exactly 1,000 rows. Spark, a program for big data jobs, introduced the idea, and its Structured Streaming still works this way by default (lesson 8).

The price is waiting, on a fixed beat. A row waits for the end of its batch: 50.5 ms on average with batches of 100 ms (a ms is a thousandth of a second). Spark's docs put the floor at about 100 ms from input to output. A batch is also a window, a slice of time, measured in processing time (when the program reads a record), whether you want one or not. A count over 5 minutes of event time, when the payment really happened (Time in streams: event time, windows and watermarks, lesson 4), spans many batches. So its state must be carried from batch to batch and saved with each one, and the state problem is back.

Micro-batches buy safety by making every row wait. Next, we'll see how a program that handles each payment at once can save its state without stopping.

try.title: Crash a record-at-a-time job and a micro-batch job
steps: From the labs folder, run MicroBatchDemo with the command below. It needs only the JDK, the kit that compiles and runs Kotlin and Java. It's plain Kotlin on a pretend clock that the program moves forward itself, so it finishes in a moment.
Before you run it, predict how many rows the record-at-a-time version writes twice. It commits its offset after payments 100, 200, ..., 900, and dies right after writing the row for payment 950.
Then explain the micro-batch version's average wait of 50.5 ms.

code.title: MicroBatchDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.stream.l07.demo /** * 1,000 payments arrive, one per virtual ms, and the job writes one output row per payment. It crashes just after * payment 950 and restarts from what it committed. Two designs: * * - record at a time: write each row at once, commit the input offset after every 100 records (at-least-once). * - micro-batches of 100 ms: keep a batch's rows in memory, then make the rows and the batch's end offset durable * in one step (Spark writes the batch's output, then its commit-log entry). A crash mid-batch leaves nothing of it. */ fun main() { val payments = 1_000 val crashAfter = 950 // record at a time val rows = mutableListOf<Int>() // durable: what the world sees var committed = 0 // durable: the committed offset var crashed = false var p = 0 while (p < payments) { if (!crashed && p > crashAfter) { crashed = true; p = committed; continue } // crash, restart from the offset rows += p if ((p + 1) % 100 == 0) committed = p + 1 p++ } println("record at a time: ${rows.size} rows for $payments payments, ${rows.size - rows.toSet().size} duplicates, " + "a row is visible right after its payment") // micro-batches of 100 ms val visible = mutableListOf<Int>() // durable: what the world sees var batchEnd = 0 // durable: the commit log, the end offset of the last batch var waited = 0L crashed = false var start = 0 while (start < payments) { val end = minOf(start + 100, payments) val batch = mutableListOf<Int>() // in memory until the batch commits for (q in start until end) { if (!crashed && q > crashAfter) { crashed = true; break } batch += q } if (batch.size < end - start) { println("crash in the batch [$start, $end): ${batch.size} rows in memory are lost; rerun the batch from offset $batchEnd") start = batchEnd continue } visible += batch // the batch's rows and its commit entry: one step batchEnd = end waited += batch.sumOf { (end - it).toLong() } // payment q arrives at q ms and shows up when the batch ends start = end } println("micro-batches: ${visible.size} rows for $payments payments, ${visible.size - visible.toSet().size} duplicates, " + "a row is visible %.1f ms after its payment on average".format(waited.toDouble() / payments)) }

try.expect:
record at a time: 1051 rows for 1000 payments, 51 duplicates, a row is visible right after its payment
crash in the batch [900, 1000): 51 rows in memory are lost; rerun the batch from offset 900
micro-batches:    1000 rows for 1000 payments, 0 duplicates, a row is visible 50.5 ms after its payment on average

The record-at-a-time version had written rows 0 to 950 when it died, with offset 900 committed. So it read 900 to 950 again: 51 rows written twice. The micro-batch version had the same 51 rows in memory, not yet visible. The crash threw them away, and the rerun of the batch wrote each one once. A payment that arrives at the start of a 100 ms batch waits about 100 ms, and one at the end about 1 ms: 50.5 ms on average.

aside.title: Why not save the count and the offset after every payment?
aside.html: You could, if both lived in one store that saves them together, in one transaction (a group of writes that is saved whole or not at all). Each save then waits for the disk, and often for a trip across the network: say a millisecond. At 10,000 payments a second, saved one after another, that's ten seconds of waiting for every second of payments (the numbers are made up for the example). Micro-batches and checkpoints spread one save over many records: one per batch, or one every few seconds. They pay with a replay instead, since a crash repeats the work since the last save.

sections.h: A snapshot of a running program, taken with markers in the stream
sections.html:
Flink takes the other road. It's a stream processor that runs across many machines and handles each record the moment it arrives. A Flink program, called a job, is a chain of steps called operators. Sources read the input, here two Kafka logs of payments. A counter keeps the count per card. A sink, the last step, writes results out to the world. Between two steps runs a channel, a queue where records wait in the order they were sent.

Every few seconds, Flink saves a snapshot of the whole job: every operator's state, plus every source's offset. A saved snapshot is called a checkpoint. After a crash, every operator loads the last checkpoint, and every source rewinds to the offsets in it.

Picture yourself at a desk, counting receipts from two shoeboxes, with a tally per card on a sheet. Every so often, you note the tally and how far you've got in each box, to come back to after an interruption. The note only works if the tally and the two places describe the same moment. If the tally includes five receipts the note says you haven't reached, you'll count them twice. In stream terms, a snapshot is consistent when every record counted in the state comes before the saved offsets, and none after them.

Version 1: stop the sources, wait until every channel is empty, save everything, start again. It's consistent, and the whole job stops for seconds at every checkpoint.

In 1985, Chandy and Lamport showed how to take a consistent snapshot of many programs passing messages, without stopping any of them. The trick is a marker, a special message sent along the channels. A program that starts the snapshot, or receives its first marker, saves its own state and sends a marker on every channel out of it. On each of its other incoming channels, it also saves the messages that arrive before that channel's marker: messages already on their way, called the channel's state. All these saved states together form a consistent snapshot. In the shoebox picture, a marker is a coloured card slipped into each box.

Flink adapts this to its jobs, and calls its version asynchronous barrier snapshotting (Carbone and others, 2015). A part of Flink called the coordinator tells every source to put barrier n, its marker for checkpoint n, into its stream. Each source writes down its offset as it does. Barriers never overtake records, so barrier n splits every stream into before and after checkpoint n. An operator with one input saves its state when barrier n arrives, and passes the barrier on.

An operator with two inputs aligns. Once barrier n arrives on one input, it stops reading that input until barrier n has arrived on the other too. Then it saves its state and forwards the barrier. That's you at the desk: you reach the coloured card in box A, so you stop taking from box A until you reach the card in box B. Alignment keeps the channels' state empty, so Flink saves only each operator's state, never records on their way. It writes that state to durable storage in the background while processing goes on, which is what asynchronous means here. The checkpoint is complete when every sink has acknowledged barrier n.

The desk picture breaks in one place. You count alone, and you can pause whenever you like. Flink's operators run on different machines and never pause together, so the barriers do the lining up that you do in your head.

In the lab's model, consistency is a one-line check: in every aligned snapshot, the records counted equal the sum of the source offsets. The stepper below runs one checkpoint, a crash and a restore.

Waiting at the coloured card makes the snapshot right. It's also waiting. Next, we'll measure that wait, and turn it off.

stepper.title: One aligned checkpoint, a crash and a restore
stepper.intro: Two sources, a counter with two inputs, and a sink that writes in transactions (txn for short). Chips are records (c1 is a record for card 1) and barriers (B1).

try.title: Read the checkpoints of a job that crashes
steps: Run SnapshotDemo from the labs folder. It runs the lab's job: two sources of 50 records each, a counter, and a sink that writes in transactions. It aligns barriers, takes a checkpoint every 20 ms of pretend time, and crashes at 160 ms.
Check the last column against the offsets on every line. What rule do they follow?
Checkpoint 3 is missing, and checkpoint 4 has the same offsets as checkpoint 2. Work out why from the crash line.

code.title: SnapshotDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.stream.l07.demo /** * The lab's job with aligned barriers and a transactional sink: two sources of 50 card records each, a keyed * counter, a checkpoint every 20 virtual ms. It crashes at 160 ms and restarts from the last completed checkpoint. */ fun main() { val inputs = listOf(List(50) { "card-${it % 3 + 1}" }, List(50) { "card-${it % 2 + 2}" }) val job = Job(inputs, aligned = true, sink = { TransactionalSink(it) }, seed = 1).run(crashAt = 160) println("checkpoint source offsets counter state records counted") for (s in job.completed) { println("%-11d %-15s %-38s %d".format(s.id, s.offsets, s.counts.toSortedMap(), s.counts.values.sum())) } println("crashed at 160 ms; restarted from checkpoint ${job.restoredFrom}") println("finished at ${job.now} ms: ${job.external.size} updates written, ${job.duplicates()} duplicates") println("final counts ${job.finalCounts().toSortedMap()}, truth ${job.truth().toSortedMap()}") }

try.expect:
checkpoint  source offsets  counter state                          records counted
1           [4, 5]          {card-1=2, card-2=4, card-3=3}         9
2           [9, 7]          {card-1=3, card-2=7, card-3=6}         16
4           [9, 7]          {card-1=3, card-2=7, card-3=6}         16
5           [14, 12]        {card-1=5, card-2=11, card-3=10}       26
6           [28, 32]        {card-1=10, card-2=25, card-3=25}      60
7           [50, 50]        {card-1=17, card-2=42, card-3=41}      100
crashed at 160 ms; restarted from checkpoint 2
finished at 424 ms: 100 updates written, 0 duplicates
final counts {card-1=17, card-2=42, card-3=41}, truth {card-1=17, card-2=42, card-3=41}

In every checkpoint, the records counted equal the sum of the offsets (4 + 5 = 9, 9 + 7 = 16, and so on): the state holds exactly the records before the barriers. Checkpoint 3 was still in progress at 160 ms and died with the job. The job restarted from checkpoint 2, and checkpoint 4 began at once, before the sources had moved, so it saved the same position. Checkpoint 7 is the last one, at the end of the input. The run is deterministic, the same every time: the same seed, the number that sets up its random choices, gives the same lines on any machine.

sections.h: Alignment costs time, and skipping it costs correctness
sections.html:
Alignment isn't free. While the counter waits for barrier n on the slow input, the fast input sits blocked, and its records pile up in the channel. In the next Try it, inputs spent about 68 ms of pretend time per run blocked by alignment.

In a real job, when one step can't keep up, records pile up in front of it, and the steps before it slow down to match. This is called backpressure. Under backpressure, a barrier waits behind megabytes of records, checkpoints take minutes, and they can time out: Flink gives up on a checkpoint that takes too long.

There are two ways around the wait.

The first is to skip alignment. Flink's AT_LEAST_ONCE checkpointing mode keeps reading every input after a barrier arrives, and saves the state when the last barrier is in. The snapshot then counts records from after the barrier on the fast input, but the saved offset still points before them. A restore replays them and counts them again. In the Try it, 152 of 178 snapshots taken without alignment were inconsistent, and 23 of 30 crashed runs ended with counts that were too high.

The second way is the unaligned checkpoint. Here the barrier jumps ahead of the records waiting in the channel, and the operator saves those overtaken records as part of the snapshot. That is Chandy and Lamport's channel state, the very part alignment existed to avoid. The checkpoint finishes quickly even under heavy backpressure. It stays exactly-once, because a restore replays the saved records before reading on. The cost is size: every snapshot carries records on their way too, so it writes more and restores more.

One default catches people out. Checkpointing in Flink is off until you set an interval (execution.checkpointing.interval). A job without one has no snapshot to restore, so a restart begins with empty state, every count back at zero.

The counts come back right now. But before the crash, the sink had already written results out to the world. Next, we'll see what happens to them.

try.title: Turn alignment off
steps: Run AlignmentDemo. It runs the same job with 30 different seeds, so the two inputs take turns in 30 different orders, once with alignment on and once with it off. Every run crashes at 160 ms.
Predict before you read: with alignment off, will every snapshot be inconsistent? Will every crashed run count too high?

code.title: AlignmentDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.stream.l07.demo /** * The same job, with and without barrier alignment, over 30 seeds (30 different interleavings), each crashing at * 160 ms. Counts snapshots that hold records past their own offsets, runs whose final counts are too high, and the * time inputs spent blocked while the counter aligned. */ fun main() { val inputs = listOf(List(50) { "card-${it % 3 + 1}" }, List(50) { "card-${it % 2 + 2}" }) println("alignment snapshots inconsistent runs overcounting blocked ms per run") for (aligned in listOf(true, false)) { var snapshots = 0 var inconsistent = 0 var overcounting = 0 var blocked = 0L for (seed in 1L..30) { val job = Job(inputs, aligned, sink = { AppendSink(it) }, seed = seed).run(crashAt = 160) snapshots += job.completed.size inconsistent += job.completed.count { it.counts.values.sum() != it.offsets.sum() } if (job.finalCounts().any { (k, n) -> n > job.truth().getValue(k) }) overcounting++ blocked += job.blockedMs } println("%-10s %-10d %-13d %-18s %.1f".format(if (aligned) "on" else "off", snapshots, inconsistent, "$overcounting of 30", blocked / 30.0)) } }

try.expect:
alignment  snapshots  inconsistent  runs overcounting  blocked ms per run
on         195        0             0 of 30            68.5
off        178        152           23 of 30           0.0

With alignment, no snapshot ever counted a record past its offsets, at the cost of about 68 ms per run with an input blocked. Without it, nothing waits, but most snapshots counted records the sources will send again. Not every crash counts too high: if a run restores from a snapshot that happened to be consistent, or crashes before any checkpoint, the replay is clean. That's why this bug survives testing.

sections.h: Exactly-once stops at the sink: idempotent and transactional writes
sections.html:
A consistent snapshot makes the state exactly-once. The output is another matter. Between checkpoint n and the crash, the sink already wrote updates to the outside world, say rows in a table. After the restore, the job replays those records and writes their updates again. In the next Try it, aligned checkpoints with a sink that appends every update get the counts right, and still 318 of the 3,318 updates written are duplicates.

There are two fixes.

An idempotent sink makes the second write harmless. Idempotent means that doing something twice leaves the same result as doing it once. One way is to upsert by key: write the card's row if it's new, and overwrite it if it's there, so a replayed count writes the same value again. Another is to store the input offset, or an event id, next to each value, and skip anything already there. Both assume the replay is deterministic: the same records, in the same order, give the same results.

Remembering ids costs space. Segment, a company that collects events from apps and websites, found 0.6% of its events were repeats, mostly from phone apps retrying. Its store of seen ids, in RocksDB (a small database library that keeps data in files on local disk), held about 60 billion after three months: 1.5 TB.

A transactional sink makes the output part of the checkpoint, with the two-phase commit of the Transactions track (Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA). It writes each checkpoint's output into an open transaction, a group of writes that becomes visible all together or not at all. On barrier n, it pre-commits: it writes everything out so the commit can't fail later, and acknowledges. When the coordinator says checkpoint n is complete, it commits. Flink's Kafka sink works this way in exactly-once mode, with Kafka's own transactions. Readers with the setting read_committed, which hides anything not yet committed, see each checkpoint's results only once it completes, so every result waits up to one checkpoint interval. In the Try it: 3,000 updates for 3,000 records, no duplicates.

Kafka Streams, a library for stream processing that runs inside your own program, gets there without barriers (the Messaging track's lesson Transactions and exactly-once). After each commit interval, 100 ms by default in this mode, three things go into one Kafka transaction: its output, the changes to its state, and its input offsets. All three commit together or not at all (lesson 5).

Confluent, the company founded by Kafka's creators, measured the cost in 2017. With 1 KB messages and 100 ms transactions, a producer (a program that writes to Kafka) lost about 3% of its throughput, the messages it writes per second. That's against acks=all, Kafka's safest setting without transactions. Kafka Streams with exactly-once lost 15 to 30% at a 100 ms commit interval, and almost nothing at 30 seconds.

The edge stays where it was. The counter in the Try it emails the cardholder when a card's count reaches 10. Every setup sent 135 or 150 emails where 90 were due (30 runs, three cards each). A side effect is anything a job does to the world outside its sink: an email, a call to the card's bank, a write to some other database. Kafka can't make such a write part of its transaction either (Go deeper has the details).

A side effect inside the job repeats on every replay. Move it behind the sink. Write "email this cardholder" as an output record, and let a separate program send it: the outbox idea of lesson 2. Give the record an idempotency key, a unique id the receiver checks, so that it acts only once.

The answers survive a crash now. Next, we'll time the restart.

try.title: Four setups, one crash
steps: Run SinkDemo. It runs all four pairings of alignment (on or off) and sink (one that appends every update, or a transactional one), 30 seeds each, every run crashing at 160 ms. The counter also sends an email whenever a card's count reaches 10.
Predict which row has no duplicates and right counts. Then predict whether any row sends exactly 90 emails.

code.title: SinkDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.stream.l07.demo /** * Four setups, 30 seeds each, every run crashing at 160 ms. For each: the updates the outside world received, how * many of them were duplicates, the runs that ended with wrong counts, and the alert emails sent. The counter sends * an email (a side effect outside the job) whenever a card's count reaches 10. Three cards, so 3 emails is right. */ fun main() { val inputs = listOf(List(50) { "card-${it % 3 + 1}" }, List(50) { "card-${it % 2 + 2}" }) val sinks = listOf("append" to { out: MutableList<Update> -> AppendSink(out) as Sink }, "transactional" to { out: MutableList<Update> -> TransactionalSink(out) as Sink }) println("alignment sink updates written duplicates runs with wrong counts emails sent") for (aligned in listOf(true, false)) for ((name, sink) in sinks) { var written = 0 var duplicates = 0 var wrong = 0 var emails = 0 for (seed in 1L..30) { val job = Job(inputs, aligned, sink, seed = seed, sideEffect = { if (it.count == 10) emails++ }).run(crashAt = 160) written += job.external.size duplicates += job.duplicates() if (job.finalCounts() != job.truth()) wrong++ } println("%-10s %-14s %-16s %-11d %-23s %d".format(if (aligned) "on" else "off", name, "$written (of 3000)", duplicates, "$wrong of 30", emails)) } println("(30 runs: 3,000 records, and 90 emails would be one per card per run)") }

try.expect:
alignment  sink           updates written  duplicates  runs with wrong counts  emails sent
on         append         3318 (of 3000)   318         0 of 30                 135
on         transactional  3000 (of 3000)   0           0 of 30                 135
off        append         3460 (of 3000)   460         23 of 30                150
off        transactional  3075 (of 3000)   75          23 of 30                150
(30 runs: 3,000 records, and 90 emails would be one per card per run)

Only alignment plus a transactional sink is exactly-once from end to end. Alignment alone makes the state right (no wrong counts), while the append sink writes 318 duplicates. A transactional sink can't save a job without alignment: the snapshot already counted records that the restore replays, and their updates are committed in the next checkpoint's transaction. And no setup sends 90 emails. A side effect inside the job repeats whenever its record is replayed.

sections.h: Where the state lives decides how long a restart takes
sections.html:
A correct restart isn't always a fast one. Every engine must get its state back first, and how long that takes depends on where the state lives.

Kafka Streams keeps state on the local disk of the machine it runs on, in RocksDB. Every change to the state is also written to a changelog topic (a topic is Kafka's name for one named log). The topic is compacted: Kafka keeps only the latest record for each key, so the log stays about the size of the store (lesson 5). The work is split into tasks, one per slice of the input. When a task moves to a machine with an empty disk, it replays its changelog first. At an effective 100 MB/s, a 50 GB store takes about 500 seconds, more than 8 minutes, and the task's payments wait.

A standby replica (num.standby.replicas=1) keeps a second copy warm on another machine by reading the changelog all the time. When a machine fails and its work moves over, a failover, the new owner replays only the last few seconds. It costs a second copy on disk, and a second reader on the brokers, the servers that run Kafka.

Flink 1.x keeps large state on local disk too, in RocksDB. At each checkpoint, it copies the state to durable storage such as S3, Amazon's service for storing files, often incrementally: only what changed since the last one. Recovering, or rescaling to a different number of machines, downloads it all back, and for terabytes of state that download is the outage.

Flink 2.0 (March 2025) added disaggregated state: the state is kept apart from the machines that compute. Its ForSt backend, the part that stores state, keeps the main copy in a remote file system. The local disk becomes a cache, a fast copy of the parts in use, and the job works on other records while it waits for a slow remote read. A checkpoint then has little to upload, and a restore little to download. The 2025 paper on it, at the VLDB database conference, reports checkpoints up to 94% shorter and up to 50% lower cost. Recovery after a failure or a rescale was up to 49 times faster. Those are the authors' measurements on their workloads, so read them as the best case.

State that only covers a short window needs neither. If a job keeps the last 5 minutes, replaying 5 minutes of input rebuilds it, and checkpointing it buys little.

All of this has a limit. Every repair here replays input, so it works only inside the engine, and only while the log still holds that input. An email can't be unsent, and a deleted record can't be replayed. Next, we'll open up the engine that does all this in micro-batches.

try.title: Size your restart
steps: A fraud-watch program built with Kafka Streams keeps 40 GB of window state per task. Its changelog restores at about 100 MB/s. How long is a task down after it moves to a fresh machine?

Now add num.standby.replicas=1. The standby lags the active copy by about 2 seconds, and the program writes about 6,000 updates a second to that task's changelog. Roughly how many records does a failover replay?
What does the standby cost you, in disk and in work for the brokers?
try.expect: 40 GB at 100 MB/s is about 400 seconds, nearly 7 minutes with that task's payments stalled. With a warm standby, the new active copy replays only what it hadn't read yet: about 2 s × 6,000 = 12,000 records, well under a second. The price is a second 40 GB copy on another machine's disk, and a second reader fetching every slice of the changelog from the brokers all the time. (The numbers are made up for the exercise; measure your own restore rate with the restore listener that lesson 5's demo used.)

refs.title: Mei et al., Disaggregated State Management in Apache Flink 2.0 (PVLDB 18, 2025)

opening:
Picture the payments app on a busy Saturday. A small program counts every card's payments. When a card has paid ten times, it emails the owner: "Was this you?" Then its machine loses power. A minute later the program is back, carrying on from where it last wrote down.

On Monday, a customer calls: she got the same email twice. The program's list of payments shows some twice too.

It's easy to think a setting would have prevented this. The tools offer one called exactly-once, which sounds like a promise that each payment is handled once. But after a crash, some payments are always handled again. A tool can only hide the repeats in what it controls, and an email isn't one of them.

In Stream joins and complex event processing, every join kept state: what it remembers between records. In this lesson, we'll crash a counting program in the middle of its work, snapshot one while it runs, and find out which repeats can be hidden. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cardholder who got the same email twice after a power cut. The counts can be made exactly right after a crash, with saved batches, barrier snapshots or transactions. The email can't, because it left the program before the program went back to its last snapshot.

Here's a question for any program you write that sends an email, charges a card or calls another company. If this line runs twice, what does the customer see? If the answer is "two of them", the action needs a key that the other side checks.

Next, we'll meet Spark's Structured Streaming, which is built on micro-batches, and find out how it decides that a window of payments is finished.

compare.title: One crash, two engines

a.label: Flink: barriers and a two-phase commit sink
a.title: Flink: barriers and a two-phase commit sink
a.html:
every 10 s     sources record offsets, inject barrier n
               operators align, snapshot state to S3
               sink pre-commits its Kafka transaction, acks n
checkpoint n   coordinator marks n complete
               sink commits: output n becomes visible
crash          in-flight state, buffers, open transaction lost
restore        all operators load checkpoint n
               sources rewind to n's offsets, replay
duplicates     none in the sink's output; side effects repeat

b.label: Kafka Streams: transactions
b.title: Kafka Streams: transactions
b.html:
every 100 ms   (commit.interval.ms under exactly_once_v2)
               output records, changelog writes and input
               offsets go into one Kafka transaction
               commit: all three visible together
crash          open transaction aborted
restore        store rebuilt from the changelog (committed
               records only), input read from committed offset
duplicates     none for read_committed readers;
               side effects repeat

compare.note: Both make the state, the input position and the output agree at one point, then replay from it. Flink lines up the whole job with barriers and keeps its state snapshots in a file store, and its sink commits once per checkpoint, so each result waits up to one checkpoint interval. Kafka Streams has no coordinator for the whole job: each task commits its own transaction, and the durable copy of its state is the changelog topic itself. That's why it can commit every 100 ms, and also why it recovers by replaying that changelog. Neither can take back an email.

worked.title: Make a Kafka Streams payment counter survive a crash, end to end

steps.say: Turn on exactly-once. Each stream thread, a worker inside the program, gets a producer that writes in transactions, and the commit interval drops to 100 ms by default. Kafka keeps its own record of transactions in an internal log, stored on 3 brokers by default. On a laptop with one broker, lower that log's replication factor (the number of copies) and its min ISR (the copies that must confirm each write) to 1. In real use, keep 3 brokers.
steps.code: val props = Properties().apply { put(StreamsConfig.APPLICATION_ID_CONFIG, "card-velocity") put(StreamsConfig.PROCESSING_GUARANTEE_CONFIG, StreamsConfig.EXACTLY_ONCE_V2) // output + changelog + offsets, one txn put(StreamsConfig.NUM_STANDBY_REPLICAS_CONFIG, 1) // a warm copy for fast failover }

steps.say: Make every reader of the output read committed data only. A consumer, a program that reads from Kafka, at the default read_uncommitted also sees records from transactions that later abort. So it sees exactly the duplicates the transaction was meant to hide.
steps.code: put(ConsumerConfig.ISOLATION_LEVEL_CONFIG, "read_committed") // in every consumer of card-alerts

steps.say: Find the side effects in the program and take them out. This foreach calls the card's bank, the issuer, to block a card, and it runs again on every replay. Instead, write a command record with an idempotency key built from the input record's identity, and let a separate consumer make the call.
steps.code: // before: runs again after every crash alerts.foreach { card, _ -> issuer.block(card) } // after: the command is output, so it commits with the transaction alerts.mapValues { card, alert -> BlockCommand(card, idempotencyKey = "block-$card-${alert.windowStart}") } .to("issuer-commands")

steps.say: Make the consumer of issuer-commands idempotent too. It reads committed commands only, and the bank's API (the interface other programs call) ignores a key it has already seen. The consumer itself is at-least-once, so a command can arrive twice, and the card is still blocked once.
steps.code: for (rec in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) { issuer.block(rec.value().card, idempotencyKey = rec.value().idempotencyKey) // safe to repeat } consumer.commitSync()

steps.say: Check the restart budget. With 20 GB of window state per task and a restore rate near 100 MB/s, a task without a standby is down for about 200 s after it moves. The standby from step 1 cuts that to the few seconds it lags behind.

lab.title: Barrier snapshots, a crash and a restore
steps: Read Dataflow.kt, which is finished: two sources, three channels, the counter, a sink, and the job that runs them on a pretend clock, picking which input goes next at random from a seed. Find where it starts a checkpoint, where it completes one, and what a crash keeps.
Run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All nine fail on the TODOs in Checkpointing.kt.

Write CountingTask.canTake and onItem. For a record, add one to its card's count and send an Update. For a barrier, mark the input as seen; once every input has delivered it, call onSnapshot with the counts, clear the marks and return the barrier. With aligned, an input that has delivered the barrier can't be read until then.

Write TransactionalSink. Updates go into the open transaction. A barrier moves it to prepared under the barrier's id and returns the id, which is the acknowledgment. onCheckpointComplete(id) appends every prepared transaction up to id to the external list, the output the world sees.
Run the tests again until all nine pass. Then read the two tests that compare setups: which one shows that the state is exactly-once while the output isn't?
hints: Save the snapshot before you return the barrier, and clear seen so the next checkpoint starts fresh. The job copies the counts you pass, so passing counts itself is fine.
prepared is a sorted map: prepared.headMap(id + 1) is every checkpoint up to id. Append its values in order, then clear() that view.
If an aligned snapshot counts exactly the records before its offsets fails, you're probably saving the snapshot on the first barrier instead of the last, or taking records from a blocked input.

drill.title: Barrier alignment from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write how an operator with two inputs handles a record, the first barrier n and the second barrier n. Then say in one line each what changes in Flink's at-least-once mode and with unaligned checkpoints.

answer.html: fun canTake(input: Int) = !aligned || !seen[input] // aligned: block an input once its barrier arrived fun onItem(input: Int, item: Item): List<Item> = when (item) { is Record -> listOf(process(item)) // normal work is Barrier -> { seen[input] = true if (seen.all { it }) { // barrier n on every input snapshot(item.id, state) // state = exactly the records before the barriers seen.fill(false) listOf(item) // forward one barrier downstream } else emptyList() // wait for the other input } else -> error("unexpected $item") } // At-least-once mode: canTake is always true, so the snapshot may include records from after // the barrier on the fast input; a restore replays and counts them again. // Unaligned: the barrier overtakes buffered records, which are saved in the snapshot as channel // state and replayed first on restore; exactly-once, but bigger snapshots.

recap: Exactly-once in a stream processor means effectively once: after a crash, records are processed again, but their effects on the state and on the committed output show once.
Micro-batches turn the stream into small batch jobs whose output and end offset are saved together. Nothing repeats, and every row waits for its batch to end: about 100 ms at the least in Spark.

Barrier snapshots (Chandy and Lamport's idea, as Flink adapted it) save every operator's state and every source's offset at one consistent point. Alignment blocks an input whose barrier came first, so no record on its way needs saving.
Skipping alignment gives at-least-once state, with some records counted twice. Unaligned checkpoints stay exactly-once by saving the records the barrier overtook, at the cost of bigger snapshots.

The output needs an idempotent sink, or a transactional one that commits when the checkpoint completes; Kafka Streams commits output, state changes and offsets in one transaction. The limit: a side effect inside the job, such as an email, repeats on replay, so it belongs behind the sink with an idempotency key.
Restart time follows where the state lives: changelog replay in Kafka Streams (standbys shorten it), snapshot downloads in Flink 1.x, and a remote main copy in Flink 2.x.

explain.prompt: A friend asks: "If Flink saves every operator separately, at slightly different times, how can the snapshot ever be consistent?" Explain barriers and alignment, and what goes wrong without alignment.
explain.answer: The snapshot isn't taken at one moment on the clock. It's taken at one position in the data. Each source puts barrier n into its stream and writes down its offset at that point, and because barriers never overtake records, the barrier splits every stream into before and after the checkpoint. Each operator saves its state when the barrier reaches it, so its state holds exactly the records before the barrier. An operator with two inputs has to wait: when barrier n arrives on one input, it stops reading that input until barrier n has arrived on the other, then saves its state and forwards the barrier. So every operator's state matches the sources' offsets, even though they save at different times. Without alignment, the operator keeps reading the fast input after its barrier. Its snapshot then counts records whose offset was saved before them, and after a restore those records are replayed and counted twice. Unaligned checkpoints fix that another way: they save the records the barrier overtook as part of the snapshot.

deeper.html:
Jobs with loops. Asynchronous barrier snapshotting saves only operator state when records flow one way through the job, because alignment empties the channels. If records can loop back to an earlier step (a job that repeats a calculation until it settles), the paper also saves the records on the loop during the snapshot, which is Chandy and Lamport's channel state again.

Other engines. RisingWave, a database built for streams, also moves barriers through its jobs and offers exactly-once sinks coordinated with them. Materialize, another, gives every update a logical timestamp, a number that orders changes without a clock, and answers queries at one consistent timestamp. Spark's micro-batches write offsets/ before a batch and commits/ after it, and lesson 8 shows the replay. Spark 4.3's real-time mode keeps exactly-once for state, but its built-in Kafka sink is at-least-once.

Small print from Flink. A job built only from map, flatMap and filter, steps that each take one input and change or drop records one at a time, has no operator with two inputs. Nothing needs aligning, so even the AT_LEAST_ONCE mode stays exactly-once there. Savepoints, the snapshots you take by hand before an upgrade, are always aligned.

Kafka and other databases. Kafka can't take part in a database's transaction today. KIP-939, a Kafka improvement proposal that would let Kafka join a two-phase commit, was accepted, but its API isn't in Kafka 4.4. Until it ships, the outbox and idempotency keys are the way across.

Transactions are only as good as their protocol. In 2024, Jepsen, a project that tests databases by breaking them on purpose, was testing a system that speaks Kafka's language. It found aborted reads, lost writes and torn transactions in Kafka's own transaction protocol (KAFKA-17754, since folded into a ticket about duplicates under exactly_once_v2). Treat the guarantee as something to test in your own failure drills, not only to switch on.

The book's version. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 12, covers micro-batching, checkpointing, atomic commit, idempotence and rebuilding state after a failure. Read it for the big picture, and the Flink and Chandy-Lamport papers for the mechanism.
